The best chain on Garnet right now is QB7-QB12-QB11, with QB12 in the middle. I ran a 3-qubit GHZ circuit on those three qubits on the Garnet simulator (garnet:mock), which is free. The simulator returned counts that do not look like a GHZ state. That is a known behavior of the simulator and does not mean the circuit is wrong.

How I picked the chain: I read the current default calibration of the real Garnet machine (calibration set 9069c4ef-7ab6-4e50-be4f-c91d71c3a06d, measured at about 16:38 UTC on 2026-10-22). It lists 30 qubit pairs that can run the two-qubit CZ gate. For each pair, it gives a CZ fidelity from a test called interleaved randomized benchmarking (IRB). I checked every chain of three linked qubits and multiplied its two pair fidelities. The best pairs are QB7-QB12 at 0.99907 and QB12-QB11 at 0.99945. Their product is 0.99852, which is the highest of all chains. The next best chain is QB17-QB12-QB11 at 0.99818.

What I ran: The circuit puts QB12 into an even mix of 0 and 1. Then it copies that state onto QB7 and onto QB11. Each copy uses one CZ gate with a single-qubit rotation before it and after it. The circuit uses exactly 2 CZ gates, on QB12-QB7 and QB12-QB11, and it measures all three qubits. I read the circuit back from the server to confirm this. A perfect quantum computer would give 000 half the time and 111 half the time, and nothing else. That result is the GHZ principle: all three qubits are linked, so measuring one tells you the other two.

Result: job 01a16482-a629-7095-b2c9-11b8351a8822 finished with 200 shots. Bits are listed in the order QB7, QB12, QB11. The counts were 000: 54, 001: 39, 110: 52, 111: 55. The simulator makes up its counts without running the circuit, so 001 and 110 appear here. On the real machine, I would expect most shots to be 000 or 111. The real run would have cost credits, and you asked for the simulator.
